message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Symbol** | H |
| **Common isotopes** | H‑1 (protium, 99.98 %), H‑2 (deuterium, 0.02 %), H‑3 (tritium, trace) |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average weighted by natural abundance) |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (0.00008988 kg m⁻³) |
| **Molar volume at STP** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| **Molecular form** | Diatomic (H₂) under normal conditions |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| **Heat capacity (Cp)** | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 298 K) |
| **Thermal conductivity** | 0.1805 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 300 K) |
| **Electrical conductivity** | Very low in neutral state; becomes conductive when ionized (plasma) |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; reacts with oxygen to form water vapor (exothermic) |
| **Reactivity** | Forms hydrides with metals (e.g., NaH, CaH₂); reacts with halogens (forming HX) and acids (forming HX + H₂) |
| **Acid–base behavior** | Acts as a weak acid (HX → H⁺ + X⁻) in aqueous solution; forms hydronium ions (H₃O⁺) |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) – key in astrophysics |
| **Isotopic effects** | Deuterium and tritium have slightly higher boiling/melting points and lower zero‑point energies; used in nuclear fusion research |

**General Notes**

- Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe, primarily found as H₂ gas in interstellar space and in planetary atmospheres.
- Its low mass gives it a very high specific heat capacity and excellent thermal conductivity relative to other gases.
- In chemistry, hydrogen’s ability to form covalent bonds with many elements makes it central to organic molecules, fuels, and industrial processes.
- Isotopic variants (D, T) are crucial in nuclear fusion experiments (e.g., D–T fusion) and in tracing biochemical pathways.
